input: The budget position has, unfortunately, deteriorated further during the current period, and it is now necessary to report an overrun that currently stands at 7 weeks against the planned position. The principal cause of this overrun lies in the EPC packages, where prices that were eventually settled with vendors came in materially above the tender allowances that had been carried in the estimate, and this effect has worked its way through the forecast in a progressive manner. A number of smaller estimating gaps have also contributed at the margins, although the settled package prices remain the dominant driver by a considerable distance. In terms of mitigation, it is proposed that further scope changes should be frozen for the time being, so that no additional commitments are entered into while the forecast is being rebuilt, and it is suggested that this freeze should remain in place until a revised and fully reconciled forecast can be presented. Responsibility for the mitigation is assigned to the project board, which would decide when the freeze can be lifted and for approving any exceptions that may be brought forward in the meantime. The position is therefore a serious one, and the 7 weeks in question will not be recovered by optimism alone; they will have to be managed through the controls that are now being put in place, together with a clearer line of sight over the packages that have still to be settled, where further movement of a similar kind cannot at this stage be ruled out.
target: The overrun now stands at 7 weeks. Its cause sits in the EPC packages: prices settled with vendors came in above the tender allowances carried in the estimate, and the difference has moved the forecast as each package has closed. Smaller estimating gaps add to the total but do not drive it; the settled package prices do. One mitigation is proposed. Scope changes are frozen from this point, so no new commitments enter the forecast while it is rebuilt, and the freeze holds until the project board has seen a revised forecast that reconciles the settled prices against the remaining allowances. The project board owns the mitigation: it lifts the freeze, and it approves any exception requested while the freeze is in place. Without the freeze, the rebuilt forecast would be overtaken by new commitments before the board could act on it, and the 7 weeks would grow by the same route that produced them. The freeze also protects the packages still to be settled. Their prices will move the forecast again when they close, and a forecast rebuilt once, against a fixed scope, can absorb that movement as a single identified change instead of as a drift. What the freeze cannot do is recover time already lost: the overrun is in the settled prices, not in future behaviour, and the board's decision is about containing the remainder of the programme, not about revisiting commitments that are already priced and placed.
